title: Conjugate Priors
interviewAnswer: A prior is conjugate when the posterior stays in the same family after multiplying by a likelihood. Beta with Bernoulli/Binomial updates successes and failures; Gamma with Poisson updates shape by total counts and rate by exposure; Normal with known-variance Normal likelihood combines means by precision. Conjugacy gives exact, fast, sequential updates and useful test fixtures, but the likelihood and prior still need to fit the domain. Check rate-versus-scale conventions, predictive calibration, and whether drift or hierarchy requires a richer model.
keyPoints: Conjugacy is algebraic closure under updating
Computational convenience never replaces model criticism
why: Conjugate models reveal the mechanics hidden inside general inference engines. A conversion posterior updates two counts; a Poisson-rate posterior updates count and exposure; a Gaussian posterior averages prior and sample information by precision. These formulas support real-time risk estimates and serve as golden tests for MCMC or variational systems. Misuse appears when teams call a prior 'ten observations' despite a mismatched population, confuse Gamma rate and scale, or force a single-rate Poisson model onto overdispersed counts solely to keep conjugacy. Interviewers test the updates, but engineers must also know what happens when traffic drifts, exposures differ, or groups share information. Exact inference in the wrong model is exactly wrong.
intuition: Conjugate priors are containers designed to hold exactly the summaries that the likelihood adds. For coin flips, the likelihood contributes a power of p for each success and a power of 1-p for each failure; the Beta prior already has those powers, so exponents add. For Poisson counts, the likelihood contributes total count to the power of the rate and exposure to exponential decay; the Gamma prior has the same form. For a Gaussian mean, information is precision, inverse variance, so prior and data centers combine in proportion to their precision. The posterior distribution retains uncertainty; using only its mean would discard the remaining spread.
deepDive: Conjugacy follows from multiplying kernels. Constants independent of the parameter can be discarded to identify the posterior family, then the family's normalizing constant restores a probability distribution. The update state is usually a set of sufficient statistics.
workedExample: A service observes 12 incidents over 30 machine-days. Prior lambda~Gamma(shape=2,rate=10), mean 0.2 incidents/day. The posterior is Gamma(14,40), mean 0.35. The MLE 12/30=0.4 is shrunk toward prior information. For ten future machine-days, prediction integrates lambda; its variance exceeds a Poisson with fixed rate 0.35 because rate uncertainty contributes. If machines have different baseline risks or incidents cluster, use a hierarchical or overdispersed model. Before implementation, verify that the library's Gamma second parameter is rate 40 or scale 1/40.
commonMistakes: Treating conjugacy as evidence that the likelihood or prior is appropriate.
Confusing Gamma rate and scale or Normal variance and standard-deviation arguments.
Reading prior hyperparameters as literal sample counts without exchangeability or source justification.
Using a fixed-rate plug-in predictive distribution instead of integrating posterior uncertainty.
Discarding raw time, group, or covariate information needed to detect drift and heterogeneity.

followUps.question: Why are conjugate updates easy to stream?
followUps.answer: The posterior is summarized by fixed-size hyperparameters updated by additive sufficient statistics. Disjoint batches can merge their counts/exposures, provided the likelihood assumptions and data lineage remain valid.

followUps.question: What is the predictive distribution for Beta–Bernoulli?
followUps.answer: The next Bernoulli success probability is the posterior mean. A batch future count follows Beta–Binomial, which includes extra variance from uncertainty in p.

followUps.question: When should you leave conjugacy?
followUps.answer: When relevant heterogeneity, covariates, dependence, censoring, mixture structure, drift, or a scientifically appropriate likelihood cannot be represented by the conjugate model.

production: Define distribution parameterization explicitly in code and tests: shape/rate versus shape/scale, variance versus SD, exposure units, and support. Maintain sufficient-statistic lineage with unique event IDs and batch cutoffs so updates are idempotent. Reconcile distributed aggregates with source totals. Monitor posterior mean and spread, predictive calibration, dispersion, zero frequency, exposure mix, group heterogeneity, prior influence, and drift. Keep a richer holdout or residual view because sufficient statistics cannot reveal every model violation. Version priors and reset/discount rules; stationary conjugate accumulation can become dangerously overconfident under changing regimes. Protect small-group rates. Provide a validated analytic fallback when a heavier inference service fails, but label its assumptions. Rollback restores hyperparameters and the exact evidence watermark, not only a displayed mean.
description: A conjugate prior produces a posterior in the same distribution family as the prior for a chosen likelihood. Conjugacy turns Bayesian updating into hyperparameter arithmetic, making it valuable for intuition, streaming updates, exact benchmarks, and low-latency systems. It does not make a prior objectively correct or every model realistic. This chapter derives Beta–Binomial/Bernoulli, Gamma–Poisson, and Normal–Normal updates, interprets pseudo-counts and precision weighting carefully, and explains posterior predictive distributions, exponential-family structure, improper limits, and when conjugacy becomes a modeling trap. You will learn how parameterization conventions change formulas, why sufficient statistics enable constant-memory updates, how prior strength differs from sample size under heterogeneous data, and when mixtures or hierarchical priors preserve flexibility. The worked examples cover conversion and event-rate estimation. The lab implements Beta–Binomial and Gamma–Poisson updates, checks batch-order invariance, and verifies moments against SciPy. Production guidance covers parameterization tests, numerical bounds, nonstationarity, prior versioning, predictive calibration, and analytic fallbacks.
learningObjectives: Derive posterior hyperparameter updates for common conjugate likelihood–prior pairs.
Interpret hyperparameters through sufficient statistics without overclaiming literal prior sample size.
Compute posterior predictive distributions and distinguish them from plug-in likelihood predictions.
Recognize parameterization, support, misspecification, and nonstationarity cases where conjugacy should not drive model choice.

deepSections.title: Beta–Bernoulli and Beta–Binomial
deepSections.body: With p~Beta(a,b) and k successes in n Bernoulli trials, the likelihood kernel p^k(1-p)^(n-k) multiplies the prior p^(a-1)(1-p)^(b-1), yielding Beta(a+k,b+n-k). Posterior mean is (a+k)/(a+b+n), and interior mode is (a+k-1)/(a+b+n-2). Hyperparameters can be read as prior success/failure contributions, but this pseudo-count interpretation assumes exchangeability and compatible evidence. Jeffreys Beta(1/2,1/2), uniform Beta(1,1), and domain-informed priors behave differently near boundaries. A Beta–Binomial predictive distribution for future counts is overdispersed relative to a plug-in Binomial because it integrates uncertainty in p.

deepSections.title: Gamma–Poisson for rates with exposure
deepSections.body: Let counts y_i~Poisson(lambda t_i), where t_i is exposure, and lambda~Gamma(shape=a, rate=b). The likelihood kernel is lambda^(sum y_i) exp(-lambda sum t_i), so the posterior is Gamma(a+sum y_i,b+sum t_i) in shape–rate form. Shape–scale libraries instead use scale=1/rate; confusing them changes means and simulations. Posterior mean is (a+Y)/(b+T). The predictive count over future exposure t has a negative-binomial form after integrating lambda. If counts are more dispersed, zero-inflated, seasonally varying, or dependent, a single Poisson rate may be inadequate even though the update is exact.

deepSections.title: Normal mean with known observation variance
deepSections.body: For prior mu~N(m0,s0^2) and iid y_i~N(mu,sigma^2) with sigma known, posterior precision is 1/s0^2+n/sigma^2. Posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of m0 and ybar; posterior variance is the reciprocal precision. High-variance data contribute less information. Unknown variance leads to Normal–Inverse-Gamma or related conjugate families and Student-t predictives, with parameterization details. In multivariate Gaussian models, precision matrices add, but conditioning and positive-definiteness require care. Standardization changes the prior scale, so priors must be transformed with features.

deepSections.title: Exponential families and sufficient statistics
deepSections.body: Many likelihoods can be written h(y)exp(eta(theta)^T T(y)-A(theta)). Natural conjugate priors have a matching form whose hyperparameters accumulate T(y) and observation weight. This explains constant-memory sequential updates: retain sufficient totals instead of every row. It also clarifies limits—sufficiency is model-relative. Totals that preserve all information under an iid Bernoulli model lose ordering, covariates, drift, and dependence information. Keep raw or auditable aggregates when those assumptions may be revised. Distributed systems can merge additive sufficient statistics deterministically if data partitions are disjoint.

deepSections.title: When convenience becomes a constraint
deepSections.body: Real systems may need logistic regression, hierarchical varying rates, mixture components, censoring, measurement error, or nonstationary state models without simple closed forms. Approximate conjugate tricks can hide important dependence. Mixtures of conjugate priors retain analytic component updates and provide more flexible shapes, but component weights must update too. Empirical Bayes estimates hyperparameters from data and should not be described as a fixed external prior. Conjugate posteriors make excellent unit-test or fallback models; compare their predictions with richer models rather than forcing every question into them. Prior and posterior predictive checks remain mandatory.

math: Beta–Binomial: p|y~Beta(a+k,b+n-k). Gamma–Poisson in shape–rate form: lambda|y~Gamma(a+sum y_i,b+sum t_i). Normal–Normal: s_n^2=1/(1/s0^2+n/sigma^2) and m_n=s_n^2(m0/s0^2+n ybar/sigma^2). These updates are associative through sufficient statistics. Predictive distributions integrate parameters: Beta–Binomial, negative binomial for Gamma–Poisson, and Normal with variance sigma^2+s_n^2 for a future Gaussian observation with known sigma.

workedExamples.title: Incident rate with unequal exposure
workedExamples.body: Aggregate total incidents and machine-time, update Gamma shape and rate, compute the posterior mean and predictive distribution, and test the result against the library's documented parameter convention.

exercises.prompt: Beta(4,6) prior sees 9 successes and 11 failures. Give posterior.
Gamma(shape=3,rate=5) prior sees 7 events over exposure 20. Give posterior mean.
exercises.solution: Posterior Gamma(10,25), mean shape/rate=10/25=0.4 events per exposure unit.

exercises.prompt: Why is future Gaussian predictive variance sigma squared plus posterior variance of mu?
exercises.solution: A future observation equals uncertain mean plus independent observation noise; total variance adds E[noise variance]=sigma^2 and Var(posterior mean parameter)=s_n^2.

lab.goal: Implement Beta–Bernoulli and Gamma–Poisson conjugate updates, verify batch-order invariance, and compare posterior moments with SciPy.
lab.buildIt:
def beta_update(a,b,successes,failures):
    return a+successes,b+failures
def gamma_poisson_update(shape,rate,total_count,total_exposure):
    return shape+total_count,rate+total_exposure

a_post,b_post=beta_update(4,6,9,11)
shape_post,rate_post=gamma_poisson_update(3,5,7,20)
beta_mean=a_post/(a_post+b_post)
rate_mean=shape_post/rate_post
lab.verifyIt:
assert (a_post,b_post)==(13,17)
assert abs(beta_mean-scipy_beta_mean) < 1e-12
assert abs(rate_mean-0.4) < 1e-12
assert abs(rate_mean-scipy_rate_mean) < 1e-12
first=beta_update(4,6,4,6)
second=beta_update(*first,5,5)
assert second==(a_post,b_post)
lab.shipIt: Test parameter conventions, retain idempotent sufficient-statistic lineage and data cutoffs, monitor predictive dispersion and drift, and keep analytic updates as versioned model artifacts rather than naked counters.
